You know very well that from the moment a finer ware than the Cream-color is shown at our Rooms, the sale of the latter will in a great measure be over there. The consequence then of my showing them a little,
before I am certain of being able to supply their wants would be a tantalising them, & ruining my own business. This transition is a very serious subject & what I am by no means ready to make at present & I beg you will insense our good customers of the impossibility of bringing about such great events in a little time.

One Barrel of Ale & one of Beer is for Mr. Hodgson with my compliments if you please, & the other two, if you have Cellar room for them I will thank you to give them a place, & hope to quaff a little of it with you over a comfortable pipe sometime in the Spring.

Pray give our love to your Triumvirate of Females. We are glad to hear they are well, & well employed, & be so good to tell my Sukey that I would have wrote to her, but am afraid she will have such an inundation of letters all at once that she will not know what to do with them.
P.S. Shod. not we have Omia's head? Pray let him take Mr. Banks's Islander with him to Otaheita.
Etruria, 12 of May 1776.

I congratulate my Dear Friend upon having come to a resolution respecting his Tour to France, for I think it a very comfortable circumstance to have brought such a point to a determination any way, as it gives a kind of rest, & satisfaction to the mind, & enables one to settle any little subordinate plans with more ease & certainty.

Well then - as you do not go to Paris, & Paris is so condescendingly good natured as to come to you, we must in our turn be grateful, & entertain them in the best manner we are able. For this purpose I will send you as
many fine things as you please - you shall only have to tell me when to stop; & even in that case I am not certain that I shall obey orders, 'till I have about some 15 or 20 thousand pounds worth of such things as must sell; that we may have a Jubilee year, & make a pilgrimage to Rome in company & Kiss his Holiness's sacred Toe together. And indeed if all be true that you tell me (for I own my doubts, that part of your letter reads so like Poetry) concerning the Bishops & Eclesiastics of the Romish Church, if my Faith was not very firmly established I could scarcely answer for the consequences, I assure you.
But permit me to ask you a few plain questions upon this subject.
Have you really & truly, & Bone Fide any fast, & certain orders for Groces, or sets of the Popes, & for what number?
Do you mean that we should send you our present stock of Popes as they are , or that we should first make them into sets, and how many sets dare you order us to make?
As the odd Popes in Greek St. & Etruria might happen if they were together to make up some complete sets, wot. it not be better to assemble them all together at one of the places?
We are about 9 Popes short, which Mr. Cox will give you an account of.

You shall have some Tablets soon. We have nine different Tablets which I hope we can make; none of them less than the Birth of Bacchus, & some of them much larger, but most of them want alterations, & repairs, to fit them for our blue & white Jasper. We have many other good things in the same situation. Oh! for a dozen good & humble modelers at Etruria for a couple of months. What creations, renovations, & generations shod. we make! Well - fair & softly, we must proceed with our own natural forces, for I will have no more fine modelers here, though I seem to wish for them, they would corrupt & ruin us all. I have been obliged to part with Radford. The hours he chose to work would, by the example, have ruined ten times better men than himself.
Etruria, 11th of Septr. 1776.

The Ladies who will have the honour of presenting you with this intend to make some stay in your Metropolis, and having received great pleasure from their company and conversation in the Country I could not refuse myself the additional satisfaction of recommending
them to your friendship and good offices, who, all the world knows are a passionate admirer of the good, & good natured amongst the Fair Sex, & that these Ladies may claim your attention under that idea let my grief, mingled with the sorrows of a long Group of Cousins, Aunts & Friends at parting from them testify.

One of these Ladies has spent her time amongst us in visiting, nursing, & watching over the Sick, & she may, without vanity, boast of success in her Pious labours, though it must be confessed, she is apt to make People laugh when they are not well , which you know is a sin against all decorum - But age & experience may get the better of that propensity.

The other is either a very good Girl, or a great Hypocrite, but as we are taught to err, if we must err, on the charitable side, we all verily believe her to be a good Girl, & as such we with pleasure recommend her to your protection.

A certain Gentleman in Drury Lane who shall be nameless, has some acquaintance with, &, I believe, I may say kindness for the Nurse. If you can bring them together it is ten to one but he takes her into keeping, & you may have the thanks of both. But for the other young Lady, she will not be so easily parted with.
Etruria, 28th Apr.l 1777. quite dark.

I thank my dear Friend for his last good letter of the 25th & can sympathize with him very feelingly in whatever relates to weakness of the brain , for I often feel it very mortifyingly, & to say I know nothing of this complaint! It is the only weak part of your letter, & the only thing tending that way I have seen from you of some time.

Your good offices with Dr. Enfield are very acceptable & I heartily wish they may have a proper effect, but I am upon the brink of despair upon that subject. The Revd. Mr. Taylor of Liverpool has had an invitation into Ireland, to supply the place of his father-in-law who has resigned. I suppose it is a better living than Liverpool. His Wife is an Irish woman, & has been in the Kingdom some time, & it is expected that Mr. Taylor will accept the call, the consequence in all probability will be a call to Mr. Yates to Liverpool - a place we are told of £130 a year! - If this should be the case our mouths are stopped, for who could ask a man to forego a Bishopric for a Vicarage. - However, whilst there is life there is hope say the friends of dying mortals & that you may know how the negotiation stands I enclose you copies of two letters,
which Mrs. Bentley will be so good to read to you over your bed pipe, & they may save you the trouble of taking a sleeping dose - one of them at least may have that effect. This packet comes by the favour of Miss Allen, a Lady who is going from Newcastle to pay a visit to the Lord Chancellor. I have told her that if she calls at the Rooms you will be civil to her &c. She was the late Lt. Bathursts unartificial daughter.

I wish we could hide you a while at Etruria - But I shall talk foolishly, & show my own head to be muddled - you were not made to be hid any where - you must shine out your day, & I hope a long, long summers day awaits you - I shall not allow of more than one being so much interested in this wish as
Your truly affect. friend
Etruria, 26th July 1777.

Must we not then expect the pleasure of seeing you & our dear Mrs. Bentley in Staffordshire this summer? I hope you will if possible make it convenient, & I will endeavour to return with you to Town & partake with you in the sweets of your country retreat.
We have such vicissitudes in the weather here that I have almost given up the antiquated idea of any distinct seasons. My Hay Grass is uncut, & the weather is as cold & rainy as winter.

I am now going to Newcastle to meet the heads of our congregation to try if we can settle matters, & agree to give an invitation to a minister. We have had several recommended to us, but I apprehend we shall conclude upon attempting to seduce Mr. Lomas from his flock. I have two reasons which will induce me to concur very strongly in this measure. One is my good opinion of, & respect for the
Gentleman & the other is the ample ability of the congregation at Derby to provide themselves with another Pastor, which is not the case with another Society whose minister we have had mentioned to us as not being averse to an invitation from Newcastle.
You will perhaps say we are ambitious, if not more. I own the charge, & may our success be equal to our ambition. So much for spirituals.
Etruria, 29th Decr. 1777.
I have my dear friends very kind letter of the 24th & need not tell him how flattering & pleasing it is to have his good opinion of our dear girls disposition & general behaviour.

We have recd. a very friendly letter from Mr. Edgeworth wherein he assures us that we may depend upon his sincerity in telling us that our daughter possesses an extremely good solid understanding, & is capable of learning anything we may please to teach her, & so far as he can judge has the strongest desire to improve herself & acquire proper habits, & that her obliging behaviour, & good disposition give much pleasure to himself & Mrs. Edgeworth. I have written this morning to tell Mr. E. that I cannot leave this place before Monday the 5th of Jany. & shall be detained all that day at a navigation meeting at Stone, & stop another day at least at Birmm., I shall not reach North Church before the 9th.

You may be a true prophet with respect to my boys being spoiled for the exertion of their own faculties, if they are enabled to purchase the fruit of other men's. But if I continue long enough amongst them I will endeavour, & I am sure you will assist me, to give them so much pride, & unquietness of spirit, that they shall not be content with anything other people can do for them, if they have not a hand in it themselves. They promise well in these respects at present, & I hope the good dispositions will continue & increase.

I have more reasons than one why my name
should not appear in the list, which I will tell you when I have the pleasure of seeing you, but in the mean time be so good to subscribe 10 guineas for me, or double that sum if you think proper, because I think it is a charity that should not be postponed, & if you afterwards convince me that I ought to give my name, I will do it along with two or three guineas more, which is as much as I would put my name to, if I did it now.

Our Anti-Americans now think that the war would be ended in the best manner we could wish, by granting the Americans all they have hitherto asked us for, but acknowledge this is rather to be hoped for than expected. What fools must we have been then to expend so much blood & treasure for something worse than nothing at all.
Etruria, 11th Aprl. 1778.
I am glad to hear so comfortable an account of your church which I feared was in real danger . I go hand in hand with you & you will please to do the needful for me now or at any other time.

Mr. Elers has given me an order for a little service of Dishes & plates & a terrine fit for so small a family as his but as he is unknowing in these things he leaves it to me. But he gives it as a hint for increasing our sale if we were to introduce arms, crests &c upon the ware & he has sent an impression of his own arms to paint this little set for him by. I am as much obliged to the good gentleman as if the thought was original & have written to him a fine letter by this post promising that he should have a few samples of table plates with crests & arms sent by the coach for his choice, & that when he returned the patterns & made his choice known his commands should be executed immediately.

P. S. Poor Lt. Chatham! How are the mighty fallen! His body & mind seem to keep pace with each other. It was almost a
pity to call him into life again he made his exit so much in his own way. He certainly will never again die so much to his own satisfaction.
Etruria, 15th Septr. 1778.

Not recollecting where I left off, & feeling just now very chagrinish at being stopped in my career, & not permitted to proceed in the invention of new pots & pipkins for my own amusement first, & afterwards for the emolument, & entertainment of all the world besides, because, for sooth, nobody will part with their money. - this being the case I begin my letter in abusing the world & everybody in it, for a blind, sneaking, paltry, foolish world, & in lamenting my own hard fate in coming into it at a time when people know, or practice no better.

Being thus cruelly deprived of all employment in the plastic art, & firmly believing idleness to be one of the seven-teen deadly sins, in turning my back of the pottery, I have got my face over a shell drawer, & find myself in imminent danger of becoming a connoisseur.
You can easily conceive the progress I have made in a month or two in the deep & very elaborate science of shell fancying . Having arranged my whole collection in the most systematic manner, & studied them with the nicest attention, I can tell you, at sight, the difference between a Lunar, & a Semi Lunar - a Buccinum, & a Limpet, & many other nice distinctions which you, who are not so learned in these matters as myself, would not understand, & might therefore undervalue. But this study, alas, like every other extention of the human mind, as it multiplies the avenues to our enjoyments discloses new sources of wants & anxieties, & at this present writing I find myself undone for an Echinites Spalagoides Cretaceous . A Gracirrynchus or two would make a fine addition to my class of Glossopetra, & the Pectunculus minimus triquetrus subfuscus would make me the happiest of chonchiologists. But perfection is not to be expected, & I shall make myself as easy as possible in my present situation; for why should I set my friend to diving in the great deep, hunting along the beach, or rummaging the chalk pits for what he may never find, or finding may not know their value.

I could give you a lecture upon the subject this morning with great good will, but I fear
you might wish me to ride my own hobby horse along the kings highway without attempting to mount you, vi et arms , upon him, I shall therefore wait to know if you are worthy before I do you the favour, & turn to our good friend at your elbow to pay my acknowledgements for the honour he has done me in his last review, in defending my reputation against that saucy fellow the author of The wreath of fashion . It was kindly done, & I thank him heartily, & will defend the Review - The St. James's Chronicle - The B-D-V &c &c with my latest breath. If he stands in need of a champion of any kind, I have thrown down my glove, never to take it up again, & he may at all times call upon the man with the wooden leg.

I rejoice to hear that bathing is likely to agree with our dear Mrs. Bentley, & shall be impatient to have it confirmed, & to learn that both she & yourself receive much benefit from your daily ablutions. I should send my best wishes for the rest of your good party if I thought they were not perfectly well & clever, or that dipping & washing could mend them. Pray give my love to Miss Stamford, & tell her that I wish her merry & happy - that she must not believe all the young men may say at these watering places, & to keep her head &
heart clear of such dangerous intruders, I would advise her to fill them both with innocent sea weeds, corrallines & cockle shells - From these I will at any time set her at liberty if she desires it, which is more than I durst promise if any of the former should stick to her.

THOMAS BENTLEY TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SR

text.p: Turnham Green, Decr. 18 1778.

Thanks to my dear Friend for his very affectionate & cheering Letter of the 14th., which I must reply to briefly, though with a most grateful Heart. My Head is better & worse as I think more properly or weakly about the ill usage that I have met with, or may still meet with from a Man who sets no Bounds to his Malignity when it is once excited; - or rather as my Head is better or worse I think more properly upon the Subject. A full Discussion, or one good Conversation upon it with my dear Friend would probably do me more good than any other Application: for I have not any Friend here by whose side I have been accustomed to engage & conquer; & who has the same Energy that you constantly possess, when there is occasion for it, either to promote the public good, assist your Friends, or support your own rights. I fancy I can do anything with your help; - & I have been so much used to it, that when you are not with me upon these Occasions I seem to have lost my right Arm.

Mrs. Bentley & I are much inclined to accept of your kind Invitation; & I want very much to go & examine into & settle my Affairs at
Liverpool: but as you will have all your Infantry & Relations about you soon I am afraid the Time would be inconvenient to you; otherwise we should be very glad to see all the Family happy together before the young Gentlemen return to School, & we will keep the Prospect of this Pleasure in our Thoughts till we hear from you, what Time would be most convenient, provided we should resolve to make a winter Flight. If we should undertake this Journey we must also pay our respects to our Friends at Derby, & so make a sort of running Visit of it though these short winter Days will be very much against Us.
Mrs. Bentley & Miss Stamford join in Love & respects to all the good Family with ire. truly affectionate & grateful Friend
Those. Bentley.
I had almost forgot to tell you the Sherry is excellent, & very comforting to the Heart.
Etruria, 8th of March 1779.

I thank you for the account of Dr. Priestleys last, & very curious experiments, which Mr. Warltire says are not only quite new, but likewise very interesting. I find he is a warm
admirer of the Doctors, & personally acquainted with him. He often mentions him in his lectures with every mark of honour & respect, calling him the Newton of the age, & assuring his audience that the Doctr. will be equally celebrated in future ages.

I find to my grief that I cannot make any great improvement in my present body but it will be china though I have endeavoured all in my power to prevent it. However to give the brat a name you may set a cream-color plate & one of the best blue & white ones before you, & suppose the one you are to name another degree whiter & finer still, but not transparent, & consequently not china for transparency will be the general test of china - Under this idea you may give it a name. What we may inadvertently make transparent, & white will not want any new name. It must be neither more nor less than porcelain .
Etruria, 27 Feb: 1780.

I have read my dear friends very good letter over & over & thank him for it most cordially. We will endeavour to take ourselves & distribute to the circle of our afflicted friends that comfort & consolation you so affectionately administer to us.

Since my last to you I have been talking with Mr. Lomas about a latin Master & in a conversation upon the subject, he told me that he should have no objection to teach my young men nay he should like it much & it would be an improvement to himself as well as them. I closed cordially with this proposal & he has already entered upon his office & gives the boys a good latin lesson every day. They are very fond of their Master & I hope this junction will be of service to all the parties - The boys will have a Master to their wishes & Mr. Lomas will preserve his latin & perhaps his Greek when Jack comes home - Will have some daily bodily exercise which sedentary Gentlemen are apt too much to neglect & a little help to a lean Salary.

My french master has promised me to be more regular & at the same time looks so good that I am apt to believe him so that at present I believe we must continue in the train we are
& hope we shall do pretty well. The boys are very attentive & regular in their School hours. They make great progress in their french & we have begun that language at table & shall introduce it in a few days at School. We already market in french & we shall certainly be great adepts before Mr. Potet leaves us.

I thank you for the copies of your pamphlet upon machines & congratulate you upon the very honourable testimony in its favour of so great a Master in composition as Mr. Mason. I shall be very glad to read it in print & notwithstanding you have such an authority on your side I shall not be deterred from finding every fault I can either in language or matter, nor from laying every fault I find before you, but to keep up your spirits a little under the apprehensions of my criticisms I will frankly tell you that you have little to fear from anybody else either in Lancashire or any other Shire. You know how we felt under the attacks of our Burton & Weaver antagonists upon a certain occasion - you have now equal advantage from your ground - are no novice in the use of literary weapons & I feel myself so far gifted with the second sight of the north that I do not hesitate to congratulate upon a
second equally glorious & equally complete victory.

How shall I descend from these elevated subjects down to pots & pipkins . I must however just whisper to you to desire you will circulate the whisper to Pollard & Jennings that my first attention has been to furnish polishing for the former & flummery shapes butter prints & Asparagus pans for the latter.
Park Gate Oct. 1782.

Jose has been so good to leave me room for a short Postscript, although as I wrote to Mama yesterday & news at Parkgate does not circulate quite so quick as it does at N. Castle I scarcely know how to fill it up.

Spring tide begun the morning we came & as that is so much better than the other tides I only drank the salt water one day before I ventured into the open sea which I did this morning & very courageously too considering what a great coward I am - the water is not near so cold as our bath & not very salt although eneough so to make me shut my mouth a little closer tomorrow. The Ladies here set excellent examples as the dance in with the greatest composure imaginable. Farewell love to every body & accept the same from your affectionate & dutiful
daughter S. Wedgwood.
Jose has dated his letter Wednesday but we are most of us of opinion that it is Friday Those. says it is Thursday - Who will you believe?
Park Gate, Nov. 2, 1782.
Dear Mama

I shall tell you a good deal about the yacht in which the Duke & Duchess Came who were very odd figures indeed Duchess of Portland changed hats with one of their attendants so the Ducss. had a black hat on with one black feather the other person with a white hat & about 3 lihgt brown feathers in. they got out of the ship about 4 miles from here they were rowed by 6 people in white shirts with black velvet caps & silver lions (the Dukes crest) it was a pretty sight enough.

The Duke came in the yacht, he is a plain dressed man with a wig like my papa's riding wig. Their children are the prettiest I ever saw very like their mother. The yacht is a very pretty vessel a deal of carving & gilding & the borders painted.

The cabin of the yacht is red velvet with gilt flowers, very grand indeed. Tell Mr. Lomas We like Park Gate very well & have seen Sir Alexander Scomberg (commander of the yacht) I will write to Kitty next post Our
parlours love to every body. I have no more to say but that
I am your affectionate son
Thomas. Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Pak Gate, Decr. 4th 1782.
Dear Papa

Yesterday Miss Twamley, Miss Wheeley, Mrs. Shaw Miss Mostyn Tom and I went aboard the Yacht which is at last come but did not at all answer our expectations. As soon as we got upon deck we went down a few steps into a cabin where there was two or three nursery beds for the children & their nurses, there was two doors out of this one of which led into a closet where the captain slept & the other into the state cabin which has two beds in it one for the Lord Lieutenant & Lady it is a crimson silk bed &
the other for somebody else I don't know who. The Duke & the Duchess of Portland came over from Ireland in the Yacht. When the Yacht was coming in the duchess got into the Yachts boat with 6 rowers in their shirts & black velvet caps with the Dukes crest in silver upon them. There was a gentleman in the boat that had changed hats with the Duchess. When the Duke quited the Dorset for the boat the Yacht fired 16 or 20 swivels & the same for the Duchess. The Yachts name is the Dorset. Each man has a small cabin & bed to himself. The crew is half English & half Irish when she is at Dublin the Irish stay ashore & when she is here the English stay ashore. Give my duty to Mama, love to my sisters and brother John when you write to him. I am dear Papa your dutiful son
Jose Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, March 7th 1783.
Dear Father

The rioters who were at Newcastle before you went, came here from Burslem, Henley &c. to follow a boat laden with corn, flour and barley which I believe was going to Manchester I think they had notice of it from our works, there were several hundreds of them men, women and children who followed it to Long Port & there a man jumping into the boat the boatman cut the rope & with the knife struck at the man, immediately half the mob cried put him into the canal which they would certainly have done if some gentleman had not interfered & got into another boat. Then they brought the boat in triumph to this place & lodged the contents in the crateshop; this was between 3 & 5 o'clock this evening. About half past seven four men came up to the house & asked for something to eat & drink as they were to sit up to guard the corn flour &c. John went to them & told them a great deal my mother followed and said some more & then they went off, but I don't know whether they will come back or no
- it is now 8 o'clock. Mr. Chisolm went to Liverpool early yesterday morning.
March 8th. It is now breakfast time they are all quiet & I hope they will continue so - the men did not come again last night.
I am your dutiful son
Josiah Wedgwood.
Dear Papa
I should have written to you certainly before this time, had there been anything that would entertain you, but nothing happening I must try to spin something out like you.

Before I finish this letter I will take a walk down to the Works and tell about all I see.
We have some very nice Cucumbers out of the Garden in that Shed but there are a many stole so that the Gardener wants it to be reed'ed all round & to have a door with lock & key.

We should be very much obliged to you would buy us one of Mortimer's Prints as we have drawn almost all the other & when we have drawn this that's intended to come the other will be fresh again. We are all very fond of those Prints. Breakfast is now ready so I must leave off.

I am turned Rat catcher yesterday at a penny a piece & caught four & Thomas struck one with a pikehill in the stable. They are so thick that if you stay still 5 minutes you may see 7 or 8 rats so that I expect to get a fortune very soon Mr. Webber's Cupped is moulded as well as Betson could do it which is pretty well. Mr. Chisolm will send some things to London to night by the Box. Yesterday it was very cold & this morning it has been raining. The grass is almost ready for mowing though in several places not 5 inches high & ready made into hay. We have 3 hens sitting with 16 or 17 turkey eggs so that we expect a many young turkeys. I know of 20
birds nests about the Garden which I don't think will be taken. I have learned from Mr. Webber that six of the 7 vases are finished are thrown in black & will be turned tomorrow, and sent to town with the utmost dispatch.
I have just been at the works & the house is built & is now tiling. Pray give my Compts. to Mr. and Mrs. Byerley & hope they are well.
I am your dutiful son
Those. Wedgwood.
Etruria, May 5th 1784.
Dear Pappa.

There is a pine apple that will soon be ready to eat, & the goosebury trees are full of buds almost. Miss Mulhall sends her best respects to you. Mary anne is very well & bears bathing very well. I think so how ever. When you come to Etruria will momma come with you?
Now I have dressed myself and will come back to Maryanne. She bathes every morning in a tub in the back kitchen & she bathed this morning in water almost cold.

I must now go to dinner but first beg to know how my sister's ankle does hope it is a great deal better and quite well I hope. My aunt Willets has just read it us up in a letter from Polly B. to her momma. Maryanne had been naughty or something this morning, Betty said that I should tell you & Maryanne cried out directly mamamama & smiled but she said gna gna when I asked her if she would send her love to you & endue when I asked her if she wanted to see you. Pray give my love to mama, sister, John, Mrs. & Polly, Jose and Tom Byerley. I can write but a very
short letter because of practising. Have you seen Mrs. Siddons again? If you have, did you cry? Good by papa! I must now give over & am
your dutiful daughter
S. Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, March 7 1788.
Dear Father
I should be very glad to have the books mentioned below bought & sent to me as soon as convenient.
La Comedy di Dante - Boyds translation of do. with notes historical & explanatory (I believe he has translated only the Inferno & the Comedy consists of Hell, Purgatory & Heaven).
Aminta of Tesco - Petrarch - if the latter is not too expensive a book, I do not mind it so much as the others.
I am reading the Abbey` Raynal now & never read a book that pleased me better or was more interesting.
I am Dear Father Your dutiful son
Jose. Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, March 21st 1788.

I send you in this box a piece of lead that I found melted on the top of the house yesterday morning on going up to look at that part of the roof that was on fire - there was more lead melted by the fire & a good deal of the timber is scorched - they are repairing the roof to-day - the damage is very trifling indeed as it appeared to me, I have not enquired the particulars from W. Heath.

I cannot tell how it was set on fire - it is in
the very corner of the roof over the stairs that go up to the nursery - there was a small fire in the yellow room but that could not cause it - the laundry pipe was set on fire, in the morning I think, to clean it & I suppose some sparks must have got through the slates to the timber - It was W. Greatbatch that first discovered it as he came up about 1/2 after 9 & he says that it blazed above a yard high out of the roof, it was put out however immediately - If the fire had begun 2 hours later the consequences would most likely have been bad as there was a wind which acted like a pair of bellows & we should all have been asleep.
I am dear Father Your dutiful son
Josiah Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, April 5 1788.
Dear Sir
By todays waggon I send the 2nd vol. of D Hancarville & I will very soon send you copies of what you want out of Montfaucon & Count Caylus.

I read the passage in your letter to Belfield & to Fox for a good deal of the very bad ware comes out of his room. I talked to them besides & assured them that they could not continue long, if they were so inclined, to let such bad workmanship go through their hands for that you would give up the enamelling branch here if it was not better carried on -

Belfield, as he always does, says he'll take care it shall be so no more & I hope he is serious for I said what I could to convince him that you was in earnest - Fox too promises very well & I dare say means so, but he says that he has not been long used to enamelling hopes that will be some excuse - I believe if I had said much more to him he would have cried -

In our enamelling room every man does too
many kinds of work & while that is the case our edging & lining will never be equal to what is done in London - there I believe it is the business of one man to do nothing but line & the same of edging - In order to come near the London work we must make a similar arrangement & keep as constantly to it as we can & this I have desired W. Greatbatch & Belfield to settle between them -

Another reason of the lining not being so good here is that the color has not been half ground & that you will see on looking at any of the plates - But the principal reason certainly is Belfields negligence - I hope he will mend, if he does not now I think he is incorrigible.
I am afraid the apprentices are rather above Foxs hand but he seemed to feel what you said in your letter & it will I hope rouse him. I believe he means perfectly well.
My love to all & I am Dear Sir Your very affect. son
Jose. Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR.

text.p: Greek Str. Apr. 16. 1788.

I told you a few days ago what your brother has said respecting the proposed scheme of Toms going to Rome. I have now received Mr Webbers letter on the same subject, in which he says "I mean to treat it without reserve, & must beg your pardon if I am too blunt, - as I think myself pretty well acquainted both with the degree of knowledge he has acquired of the arts, and his power to improve it, I will briefly observe, That with regard to the first he has not yet a sufficient stock to be exported to Rome, & with regard to the second I own with sincerity that I have never seen any young man possessed of more than he is. It is then my opinion, which I draw from observations made here on others, that the best method will be, to study the whole approaching summer in England, not merely design, but every other branch of taste. - This, which was ever my opinion, has been riveted in me by what I have learnt in conversation from my young countrymen here, many of whom feel very much hurt at not
being able to taste those pleasures which they see enjoyed by others on the contemplation of the works of art - But after a preparation during the summer at home, I am bold to say that four months study in Rome will be sufficient, & that without such previous preparation it is little short of being useless. - A very aimable young man told me with a great deal of sensibility, that if he could have had the most distant idea of Rome, he would have given the most assiduous application to the improvemt. of his taste, & so sensible was he of the necessity of more real knowledge of the works of Art than those who make a trade of showing them, that he engaged a painter to go round Rome with him, in preference to the best antiquary that could be found, & is trying constantly to find some painter to teach him design" -

"With respect to the effects of the seasons - in the months we have been here, we have had almost constant shiroc winds, which alone are sufficient to make life a burden - The summer must be insupportable indeed at Rome - Even at Naples, where the climate is better, several young people were at the point within the last 6 weeks - Mr Flaxman was one of them, who is now pretty well recovered" -

"As Mr. Wedgwood talks of spending the
summer in Germany, but first to see Florence & Venice, I shall accompany him there, & then return directly to England" My dear Jose:

You will see by Mr Webbers letter as well as your brothers what their united opinions now are with respect to Toms going, or rather not going to Rome, & as they will themselves be with us in the course of this summer, that renders the plan altogether impracticable.

The fluted altar flowerpot with a patera at the top, is very well executed, & a very good thing. These two articles do you credit as a potter, & will help to gain you our confidence on future orders. Give me leave to hint what appears still wanting in the flower-pots to make them complete. The top of the patera should be gilt as well as the handles, which besides making a good finish, & hiding the poverty of the top, forms a gold band which connects very naturally with the gold handles. The three little white feet at the bottom of the patera should also be gilt. Such little touches and finishings show the master in works of art, as minute attentions in behaviour show the well bred man & polite gentleman.

We have just now recd. the two smaller
sizes of pedestals, the expedition with which you have sent them will oblige Mr Parker, & is very pleasing to me. I will show them to him, & let you know what he says. They appear to me Dutch built, the lower ones especially in a very high Degree, that is, they are much too wide, particularly upwards, for their height. The young woman spinning leans forward too much, as does the woman & child on the other pedestal The little one stands very crooked, owing to the bottom square plinth being cut lower considerably on one side than the other.

I think I wrote to you before that some smelling bottles with Henry IV of France on one side, & his minister Sully on the other, would be very acceptable. The heads are too large I know for this purpose, but they will easily be made less, by sinking & taking away part of the shoulder. - The Emperor of Germany on one side & the spread eagle on the other, - for another sort.
your ever affectionate father
Jose. Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, Aug. 22 - 1788.
Dear Sir

I spent the most part of two days at Soho with M Bolton Junr & Mr. James Watt Junr. M Bolton has been at home 6 weeks or 2 months & is going on Monday into Germany where I believe he will stay some time. I think he is much improved since he went to France - the people of Birmingham expected him to come home quite a frenchman but they have been luckily disappointed.

I called on Dr Priestly & paid him £20 for
you was in arrears 2 years - he wishes to have a few vessels made for him which I will get done - his elaboratory has been robbed under the notion he believes that he refined gold & silver but nothing of much consequence has been taken.

At Mr. Boultons elaboratory they have been making some fulminating silver - it is silver precipitated by lime & afterwards washed with volatile alkali - heat is not necessary to explode this, a touch with a stick or anything else is sufficient & I believe it is not necessary that it should be dry for there happened to lye a very small quantity scattered upon the grass before Mr Bs. elaboratory & a gentleman happening to touch it with his cane it exploded & very much surprised him.
Tom joins in duty & love with Dear Sir Your affect. son
Josiah Wedgwood.
Dear Sir
For two months past I have been rambling about the country, - the Lakes - Blackpool - Matlock - in hopes of laying in a stock of health & spirits for the winter.

I must once for all, beg your acceptance of my best thanks for the early communications, from time to time, of your truly valuable discoveries, which now become more & more interesting; & I most sincerely wish you health with every convenience for the prosecution of them.

I cannot forbear expressing my particular satisfaction to find that my old favourite, Phlogiston, is likely to be restored to its former rank in the chemical world. I suppose you do not mean to exclude heat from the composition of air, but consider that as a kind of universal principle, & therefore think it unnecessary to be specified as an ingredient in particular bodies - I persuade myself that the ensuing winter will produce some further advances in our knowledge of this subject, & of the principle of acidity, which seems now to be in a very promising train of investigation.
Mr. Watt's conjecture of nitrous acid being contained in inflammable air, as the vitriolic is in sulphur, pleases me much, though I confess there is one circumstance which appears rather unfavourable to it; for I understand it to be by combustion that the acid is detached from the phlogiston, & one would expect the nitrous acid to be rather decomposed than developed by that process.

I shall be happy to see the paper you have now drawn up, but would not give you the trouble of taking a copy of it on purpose. I shall be in London in about ten days, & the copy intended for the Society may then pass through my hands, as you propose, to Dr. Heberden.

I received your letter by the chevr. Landriani & was happily at home when he visited this place; he was so good as to stay with me a day or two, & I found in him extensive knowledge, & great facility of communication, so that his company was very agreeable. He has a minute knowledge of manufactures, which, with his readiness at sketching, enables him to make every thing he sees his own, & then, you know, he may carry it where he pleases.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, May 25 - 1789.

James Lily the clay beater who has now 11/6 P~ week wishes to know whether you will allow him to stay at 12/. He says he has worked 20 years with you & it is very hard that you should now differ about /6 a week.

G Tittensor & G Riles slipmen spoke to me this morning & wish to be informed whether they may stay in their places. W Greatbatch has told them that you said you would part with them all, but as they spoke to me this morning I thought it was as well just to mention it to you. I should be glad to hear from you as soon as you can, as these slipmen have places, I believe at Rogers to accept of.

W Wood spoke to me this morning not knowing that W Keen (Heaths son in law) had spoken to you himself - to say that W Keen would be very glad to go to piece work
again & seemed to think that he had been sufficiently punished. I told him I did not suppose his being at day wages was meant now as a punishment but that you did not like the apprentices being at piece work - there are however some younger apprentices at piecework - I promised to mention it to you.

On going down to the works tonight, I find that all the painters except Jno. Steel who is come to work tonight left work at 3 or 4 o'clock, some disgust at printing I believe is the cause but I have sent for Belfield - He says that they have determined not to do the work that Belfield gave them to do - large terrines that are to match the printed ware - I told Belfield not to give them any other work but he did give them some red etruscan ware but they are determined not to do it.
I will write farther tomorrow after I have seen some of them.
Good night.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, May 29 - 89.
Dear Sir

I had said to the painters just what you now direct me to do - that printing would be their best friend & that as it was not a thing started up after you was gone, they ought to have objected to it whilst you was here or else to stay until you came back. I am glad I happened to do what was right & that it had the desired effect, for they have been very constantly at work ever since.

I desired them to state why they had an objection to printing, but this they either would not or could not do; having acted from nothing but a foolish prejudice & gone into a passion without knowing why.

I asked them whether you did not deserve better at their hands than for them to fly from their work, without saying a word as soon as you was gone. Job Meir, who was spokesman, said that they should always acknowledge that you was a very good master & that there was no fault to be found in that respect.

I mentioned your having filled a warehouse
with enamelled goods (yet unsold) rather than they should want work & said that it was very improbable that, after showing such a disposition, you should introduce printing to deprive them of the means of getting a living & that as it was your interest that cheaper, more expeditious & better ways of doing the patterns should be made use of, so it was theirs - that your interest or that of the manufactory & their real interests were necessarily connected. On cool consideration I was sure they would be convinced of it & I suppose they are.
I am Dear Sir Your dutiful son
Josiah Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, July 24 - 1789.
Dear Sir

Mr W Wood has just been to tell me that a gentleman in the pottery has sent to him to say, that, if he (W Wood) is not engaged with you for life, which he always thought till now that he was, he would wish to speak to him & the messenger said that his master would dare to give him a guinea & half a week with the privileges that he enjoys here. W Wood engages not to engage with this gentleman before your return & that he will give you the preference. He says he knows it is for your interest for you to keep him & that he will stay so long as you will make his place with you as good as he could have in another place.

Do you not think it would be proper to get some snuff box tops with the Duke of Orleans head on them. You have no doubt seen in the papers that the French have recovered their liberty & that the Duke is a very great favourite with the popular party.
I am obliged to stop for it is quite time to send my letter.
I am ever Dear Sir your dutiful son
Josiah Wedgwood. Junr.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, July 28th 1789.
Dear Sir
We are making Mr Neckers head of a size proper for snuff box tops & the Duke of Orleans the same.

Do you choose to have anything modelled of the same size which should relate to the late revolution in France & to the support given to public credit by the national assembly? What do you think of a figure of Public faith on an altar & France embracing Liberty in
the front? Mr Byerley says we ought to do something & that quickly. I will get Mr Webber to make a sketch & send it you tomorrow.

Mr Elijah Mayer brought a nephew of his here this morning whom he wishes you to take into your warehouse. He was in Mr Neales in London & had £50 P~ ann. but his health would not permit him to stay. Mr Mayer says he is perfectly sober & would not lose a day in the year except from ill health. I told him that I would write to you.
Jose Bourn has engaged a young man upon trial who used to sell ware but has given that up. Mr Mayer said his nephew would leave wages to you.
Messrs Verlingen & son of Boulogne owe us £380. I will translate a part of their letter of 24 inst

"We are Sir in very unfortunate circumstances, the crisis that France & of consequence Commerce, suffers at present, the horrid misery which ravages all the provinces & which influences all conditions, has totally suppressed circulation & sale, an over flow of goods of which we have laid in too great a stock, calculating the future sales of this year in proportion to those which last years plenty had produced & in short the delay of payments
which we ourselves have suffered under, make it impossible for us to fulfil our engagements with the exactness upon which we have until now piqued ourselves. Therefore Sir we beg you to consider our situation in the payment of what we owe you & be persuaded that as soon as the sales are renewed we will exert ourselves to the utmost to satisfy you; trust our probity & the delicacy of our sentiments. We have always endeavoured to merit the esteem of our correspondants, happy if we have obtained yours. It is at this moment especially that we have the greatest need of it & that we shall without doubt congratulate ourselves on having gained your good will & opinion."

George set out last Wednesday to buy you a horse & is not yet returned. I suppose he has got you one & has taken him on to Blackpool, as he meant to do if he got one at the farthest point he meant to go to, as he would then be near half way to you.
We shall be very happy to hear from you not having had a letter since you were at Preston.
Tom joins me in love & I am Dear Father your dutiful son
Josiah Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, July 29 1789.
Dear Sir

Enclosed is the sketch of the medallion I mentioned to you last night. The figure on the altar with the Caduceus in one hand & the Cornucopia in the other is Public Credit or Faith & instead of the caduceus on the Altar there ought, I think, to be the words Fid. Pub. for fides public , the goddess of liberty with the cap of liberty in her left hand takes hold of France in her right. The figure of hope in the Botany bay medal would come in exceedingly well for this figure of liberty & the other two would be modelled very soon. The story appears to me to be well told & to make a good composition.
I am Dear Sir Your affect & dutiful son
Josiah Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO THOMAS WEDGWOOD.

text.p: Greek St., Sunday. 1790.
Dear Tom

I am glad to hear that you have got a new addition to the stock of Roman vases and still more so as I suppose they are of a size proper to be put into immediate use by what
you say about making a set of vases with the life of Achilles. I think the idea is perfectly good. Your black tea ware with lively colours I dare say will please the foreigners, but the English I am afraid will not admire them. We are not bold enough to adopt at once anything that is new and beautiful but require the sanction of fashion to give it value.

I have no idea of what you mean by new Etruscan vases, new colours - pattern & figures. I suppose they must still be red and black but improved. If that is meant I dare say the sale of them will be considerable.

I think you are right with respect to the impropriety of adopting the whims of customers and bringing them into use; but in this matter I believe you must not be too rigid. There are many cases in which it is necessary to humour them, especially in a business which depends almost entirely upon fashion.

However it is right I think to let all whims but good ones stop with the owner and not to bring them into the warehouse as common articles of manufacture. You must consider that it has been in a great measure owing to the taking up hints given by customers and bringing them to perfection that this manufactory has established its character for Universality .

I have met with two or three of my Edinburgh acquaintance that I never was intimate with. But the other day I met Girdlestone and he has since called upon me. I mean to see him tomorrow and expect much pleasure in his conversation. I have seen Tom Jervis two or three times and find him very agreeable and clever - he is studying in the temple and means to be called to the bar.
Yours affectionately
Josiah Wedgwood Junr.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR.

text.p: Greek St., May 9, 1790.

2 trials of Barberini black. With respect to color, they are very much alike, & both very nearly the same as the vase I have with me. But in another respect, the total absence of cracks on the surface, that made of an equal
mixture of blue & black, & then dipped in black, has the preference very greatly. It is indeed entirely free from cracks, which the other is not; & as it seems to agree perfectly with both your whites, the yellow & the blue white, I would have you proceed with that in order to lose no time, & be getting more raw materials prepared. I think Dan Hollinshead & his brother should be kept entirely on the vase. For I have 20 copies subscribed for now, but this is only for yourselves, & must not be mentioned at the works for obvious reasons, I mean, that you should not mention its being greatly approved of, or many copies subscribed for - only let them go gently & steadily on with that as with any other work. But though I would have you be going on with this composition which we know will do, I wish you at the same time to be making trials with the blue clay, to make it take a black dip, without cracking; perhaps a little 59, or some ball clay, may have that good effect. The cracks are exceedingly minute, not visible when dry, even with a magnifying glass, but when the piece is wonted, they become distinguishable just before it is quite dry, by their deeper colour, the cracks retaining the water longer than the sound part of the surface.

I wish you to look at the left leg of Pluto between the calf and the ankle the latter of which is not seen, & compare it with a cast out of the mould taken from the vase itself which you will find in one of the drawers of the cabinet closet, this part is said to be too broad. If so, it must be narrowed a little.

Another deficient part in the vase I have is rather owing to accident, from the extreme thinness of the part, I mean the ham & upper part of the calf of the figure entering into Elysium, being jagged.
Some of the vases may be made with the white without any blue in it, & some with the yellow white, as I know that difft. people will have different tastes.

The theory I proceed upon with respect to cracking is this, that the black diminishes more in burning than the blue, and therefore must crack if it keeps applied to the blue in every part. As 59 mixed with the blue will cause it to diminish in burning proportionably to its quantity, to a certain degree, there is a proportion which will make it diminish exactly the same with the black; that proportion is to be found out, & the cracking is cured. I congratulate you on the success you have had in making one body, the mixture of blue & black, perfect in this respect - as also on your
success in curing the enamel kiln, which is a very great acquisition.
Mr. Byerley says, and I join with him, that you will do anything you attempt.
Mr. Webber leaves this place to return to Staffordsh. on Tuesday.

We have nothing here at present that we could employ Shufflebottom in, but mere painting of borders. Another year we might contrive something for him, & I think he had better put off his journey for a year.

With respect to the ovens, I cannot tell what to say till I come home to talk about it. As to lighting an oven on a Sunday afternoon occasionally when there may be particular reasons for it, there is not so much objection to that as to making it a constant custom & rule to fire the ovens on a Sunday. This is all I can or have time to say in writing.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, May 14, 1790.
Dear Sir

Mr Fletcher called here this morning with Mr Lomas and requested me to dine with Mr Kynnersley at his house on Wednesday and on Thursday to attend him on his canvassing. I told Mr Fletcher I wished him success but that I could not promise to go with him on Thursday without your directions; and he said he should not wish me to do so. Enclosed is a letter from him which I promised him to send. I am equally willing either to canvass with him or to stay at home. Be so good as to write to me by return of post. I believe there would have been no doubt of his success if he had declared his intentions before the Marquis members canvassed but so many made their promises then that he either cannot come in or if he does, he must be brought in by persons who have broke their words. He says himself that the lateness of his proposing does not make 10 votes difference but I believe it is not exactly so.
Your dutiful & affect son
Josiah Wedgwood.

My dear Jose. will see by the enclosed to Mr Fletcher the line of conduct which I mean to observe, - that is, the same which I have hitherto done on all similar occasions, as I do not see any good reason for altering it.

I have no vote for a member of that borough, & have therefore no specific or local reason to
interfere; & I do not know any general principle which, if valid in this instance, would not hold much farther, & claim from me a like interference throughout the county at least - perhaps far beyond.

Speaking politically, I believe you know my sentiments that so long as we have septennial parliaments, it is of little consequence who is chosen into them; they will generally, in like circumstances, so long as human nature continues the same, act as they have hitherto done. A real parliamentary reform is therefore what we most stand in need of; & for this I would willingly devote my time, the most precious thing I have to bestow, or any thing else by which I could serve so truly noble a cause.

You will say perhaps, that to accomplish this end, we shod choose independent members of parliamt. Alas! It is too certain that this object never will be obtained from parliamt. in the first instance; so long as parlt. remains on its present plan, all little partial struggles is beating the air, & wasting that time & strength which should be employed for better purposes, I mean, to promote a radical cure, by reducing the duration of parliaments to their original limits.

Mr Fletcher's political principles are, I
believe, in many respects, the same as my own, & I have long had a sincere value for him as a friend & neighbour; but I have for many years past determined to keep clear of electioneering disputes, unless I should perceive it more incumbent upon me to involve myself in them than I have yet done.

These are the principles on which I have hitherto acted, but I do not desire you to adopt them merely because they have been mine. Examine for yourself, & then act according to your honest conviction, in this & every other instance, and your conduct, whether it is the same as my own would have been in like circumstances, or the contrary, will nevertheless have my approbation.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, May 25, 1790.
Dear Sir

We are so situated with respect to our apprentices that I find it necessary to consult
you. Finding that the appces. at U W played whenever they pleased Tom sent word that they should not play without their masters leave. 6 of them seem determined to do as they please.

Some exertion of authority seems necessary here and yet they are not apprentices for there is not one of their indentures in which the terms of the act have been exactly complied with - some are not indented - others have the money stipulated for expressed in figures instead of words at length & others are not executed.

I went to Mr. Caldwell this morning to consult with him about the legality of these indentures. He read me a case in which the plaintiff, who had instituted a suit against another for enticing away his apprentice, was nonsuited inasmuch as the indenture was not indented &, consequently, not being an indenture, could not bind a person under age. It is very clear that in all cases of these 5 indentures not one is a good one. But if you was to take one of these boys before a magistrate, Mr. C says, it would be in the magistrate to take the imperfect indenture as testimony of a contract, & of its conditions, between the boy & yourself, & the boy might be considered as a servant though not as an apprentice.

It is exceedingly unpleasant to pretend to an authority which one cannot fully establish. Would it not be proper to have fresh indentures made out legally for the remainders of the different terms that the boys have to serve & if any refuse to sign them, to try what we can do with the old indentures. If nothing, I should think it much better to discharge them than to have a set of nominal apprentices who are not bound by the rules of apprentices.
I am afraid we shall suffer much from the contest as I hear the ale houses are to be opened at Newcastle & Trentham hall is so now I believe.

No mobs or murders at Ncastle as Mr B. has heard but much drinking & I suppose some fighting - one of our labourers who was got drunk in Trentham hall was so imprudent as to cry Fletcher for ever & in consequence was well thrashed.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, June 2, 1790.
Dear Sir

Will Sneyd of Belmont is now in town. His object is to get a commission if there be a Spanish war. I acquainted him with Mr Bs & my intended journey some time since & when I was at Belmont last he said he would go with us. I told him the nature of our journey & that I did not think it would be an entertaining one for him. He has written to his father that if he does not succeed in procuring a commission he would be glad to make the journey along with Mr Byerley & me, & Mr Sneyd has no objection to his doing so.

He would be very useful in travelling for from his long residence in Berlin he speaks German & I believe he speaks it well. You know too that he is of mild & gentlemanly manner & I think there are no objections to him that would not be equally strong against
any third person not connected with the business.
If you do not think that it would be proper for him to go, you will be so good as to let me know. Indeed I think it very likely that he may get a commission & then he will not wish it.
I am Dear Sir Your affect & dutiful son
Josiah Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, June 7, 1790.
Dear Sir

I was too much tired last night with writing a long french invoice to reply to your letter. I have no more desire myself to make our journey, a journey of pleasure, than you
have that it should be so, and I am very sensible of the strong distinction kept up on the continent & especially in Germany, between men engaged in business & gentlemen - but I do not at present see that all those disagreeable consequences which you are afraid of, would follow our having a gentleman in our company. Even if they did follow I think W S is more concerned in them than Mr B & myself.

In the first place I have no wish to go into any company where I must assume any other character than my own, to be treated with respect, and I see very little probability in a tour of business of our having much opportunity of entering into the society of the little gentlemen - I say little in opposition to the Princes & greater nobility.

W Sneyds intention is certainly to accompany us in the whole of the tour and he is fully apprised of our views. He has been long enough in Germany to know whether he chooses to go along with us in the character of manufacturers and consequently to submit to all the inconveniences attending such a character.

I must observe also that much of our time will be spent in the free or Imperial cities where much trade is carried on and where it
must be supposed that the character of a merchant is respectable, & it is most probable that the most agreeable society for us will be found among merchants in those cities. But our stays in the different cities will be so short as to allow very little time for any other visits but those of mere business. I should think that such a journey could not be pleasant to W S. but he is the best judge of that.

I confess there is one objection to his going with us that does not seem very willing to be overcome. I mean his being in our way and to this I do not pretend to reply but must allow it its full force.

I should think that a strong representation of the dryness of such a journey to him might perhaps cause him to decline it - if it did not I should feel myself in an awkward situation & should hardly know how to refuse his company without giving him offence which I should be extremely sorry to do. Perhaps you & Mr Sneyd might settle that matter better than W S & myself.
Give our love to all & believe me Your affect & dutiful son
Josiah Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO THOMAS WEDGWOOD.

text.p: Dear Tom

We intend to set out at the end of next week if possible & I do not think my father & mother will set out before us but I am not at all certain of this. The most difficult part of the arrangement preparatory to our journey is the leaving some one in the care of the house here, for the clerks that seem the most proper have large families & it would not be agreeable to have them, but I believe it is settled that one of them, Howship, is to sleep here & to board with his family. The correspondence, at least the greatest part of it, must be conducted at Etruria by you and your colleague. The money will I believe be sent down from Drummonds & you must draw immediately upon them, so that the cash-keeper here will have only to receive money & to pay it into Drummonds hands.
We have got the travelling chaise repaired & painted, quite plain without arms or cipher.

The revolution at Newcastle will have much the appearance of design & I am extremely
afraid that you will hardly be judged quite innocent by the Trenthamites.

You will let me know as soon as you can the result of the poll. Mr Kynnersley is much more likely to succeed than Sr. J. Chetwode & I think than even Mr Fletcher. If W. Sneyd wishes to be in parliament I should think his uncle would have a good opportunity of introducing him at the next election.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Rotterdam, July 2nd 1790.
Dear Sir

We set out yesterday from Helvoet, where we arrived after a very favourable passage of 16 hours, in a schuyt or boat with sails & 2 men, & had an exceedingly pleasant voyage up the Maese to this place. But I should
first tell you how we fared on board the paquet - In about 2 hours I began to be exceedingly sick & got into our chaise which was upon deck as being a much pleasanter birth than the cabin. After I had been there about an hour Mr Byerley introduced the honble Mr Jenkinson through the window as the doors could not be opened. As he was sick & could not well stay upon deck Mr Byerley gave up his place in the chaise to him & lay upon deck with no other covering than his great coat & travelling cloak & although it was a very wet night I have the pleasure to say that he has caught no cold. -

I was very much pleased with the appearance of Rotterdam, ships trees houses & draw bridges thrown together in a manner which must astonish every stranger - We had a letter to Mess. Jasper Atkinson & son who were very obliging to us - Mr Atkinson took us into a hardware or jewellers shop where we found a good number of our cameos mounted in steel, but we found an equal number of french imitations which are set very cheap - they are of a fine blue but it looks like smelts dusted on a soft ground & the white does not appear to me to be porcelain but wax or some
composition which will cast. I will send you one from Amsterdam. The master of the shop told us that he had some snuff boxes with cameos made at Seve which were dearer by much than ours about 2 guis. & as he says much finer not being historical pieces as ours are but fine conceits. I suppose such as we saw in London. Mr Byerley says he imagines that these cameos have stopped our snuff box business at Paris which was becoming a very fine one. We shall I dare say be able to get some more information at the Hague, where we are going this afternoon, about these french cameos & if we can get one we will send it you. Perhaps at Paris we may get such knowledge as will enable us to recover this business.

I have not yet seen enough of Dutch men & women to be able to form any ideas about them, the appearance of the women however is very striking at first sight - enormous straw bonnets - 2 black patches on the temples - very close caps - no stays, & by their bulk I should suppose they have on 12 or 14 petticoats which are however pretty short - they wear light blue or grey stockings & slippers without hind quarters - they have almost all light hair & what I should call phlegmatic complexions - neither very fair nor much color but
polish - they have not much life about them. The young boys & girls have I think a strong national character.
Your dutiful son
Josiah Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Hague, July 4th 1790.
Dear Sir

I believe I wrote to you from Rotterdam on the 2nd that we were setting out to this place - We arrived very safe at an excellent inn & acquainted Lord Auckland immediately of our being here & asked him when we should wait on him - He desired to see us immediately or early in the morning - I mean to be very particular in my account of his behaviour to us as I am sure you will be much pleased to
find that he acts here as well as else where as a very good friend to you - We found him & Lady A at breakfast & both very well - Lady A- looks I think better than she did 4 years ago - We showed the vase & they were both very well pleased with it & Lt. A began very soon to form a plan for showing it in the most respectable manner - He wrote immediately to the Princess of Orange enclosing a catalogue & begged to know when he might bring us to her to show the vase - She appointed this evening at 1/4 past 7 which Lt A- says is a great favour as this is a week of devotion when I believe they are very strict as they are in Scotland in the sacrament weeks - His Lordp asked us to dine with him on the same day - Mr Be did not go having a headache but I met there Mr Jenkinson who came over in the same packet, Mr Stanley to whose father you had shown the vase in London & Mr Crawfurd the British minister at Rotterdam - He invited us to dine with him again today which we did & met Lord Henry Spencer & Mr Jenkinson In the evening Lt A took Mr B & myself in his carriage to the Princes summer retreat about a mile from the Hague, called the house in the
wood - where we showed the vase to the Prince, Princess, & their eldest son & daughter Lord Auckland took upon himself the office of Cicerone & gave a very good dissertation upon it, insisting much upon the merit of the nuances - The princess of Orange said a few words to me about the journey that we were to make & asked if we had any thing else with us - The Prince on coming in spoke in english & either took Mr Byerley or me for you - he said "I have known you by your works but not personally before" - He afterwards asked me in French where the Manufactory was - how far from London & how long it had been carried on to all which I answered in french & Lt Auckland told me I spoke pretty well for a beginner.

Lord Auckland then begged of the Prince & Princess to breakfast with Lady Auckland tomorrow which they have promised to do & he has invited about 50 of the first people here to breakfast at the same time & there is to be a display of the Vase in one room & of the rest of our patterns in another.

It is impossible to conceive more friendly behaviour than that of Lt A- to us & we must be very suspicious not to believe that
he is sincere. He has a copy of our route & will give us letters to as many as he can - He introduced us to a Dr Maclaine, pastor of an English congregation of dissenters of some sort here who is a great lover of the arts & very much admires many of your productions - He has given us a letter to Mr Hope & Lt A will give us another - I believe you have seen Dr M.lain at least he has seen you & says a great deal more in praise of your works than I can repeat.

I forgot to mention that we took with us a couple of the heads of the present king of Prussia which Lord Auckland presented to the princess & which she said were very like - she knew the drawing that they were done from, Mr Poggi has it -
Be so good as to make some more & let them be sent as soon as possible to Hamburgh.

The prince and princess both spoke very highly of the vase though I believe the latter only had much feeling for it. The prince put me in mind of Mr Okeover though he is a less man - The princess has the look of a very clever woman & I believe she is so -

Lt. Auckland says that some friend tells him that Virgil gives a description of the gates
of death & that one of the pillars is black the other white. Lord A- thinks that if this is the case it will apply very aptly to the different colours of the vase & that Virgils having said so will not at all go to prove that the vase is of work as modern at least as Virgil, for Virgils mythology is certainly much more ancient than the AEneid - But his Lordship thinks that there is a mistake in ascribing this passage of Virgils to the gates of death - he thinks Virgil gives a description of the gates of sleep . Mr. Chisholm will look at it & as-soon as I can get a Virgil I will do the same.
July 5th 1790.

I now am to give you an account of our exhibition - About half after 10 Mr B & myself went over to Lord Aucklands & disposed all our chaise seat full upon 4 tables, one of which the collection of cameos filled. In this room there were upon the chimney piece 7 jasper vases belonging to Lt Auckland so that altogether we cut a very respectable figure. We had some few cameos mounted very handsomely in necklaces, bracelets & ear drops which we also displayed. We had a thermometer also which was much looked at & people seemed to be very inquisitive about it.

In another room was the Vase by itself & in a third & 4th, the company breakfasted. All the first people that are at the Hague were there but as the fashion is here to go into the country as it is in England there were not above 60 or 70. The prince & princess with their daughter who is to be married to the Duke of Brunswick came about half after 11 & said every thing that was to be expected. The prince talked to me a little about the time that the Etruscan vases had been made & seemed to have noticed them from the beginning. There was a gentleman there who
has made Antiques his study & he was extremely pleased with the vase but he did not agree with the explanation which you have given as to the parts though he thought the general idea was true. He thought that the figure of the man in 1st compart. from its attitude was a betrothed person who is very much concerned to die & leave his spouse & that this will account for the Amour who leads him into elysium - the figure with a staff in 1st compartt. he supposes to be the genius of Mercury that waits to lead the shade to Elysium & the figure with the serpent he calls the genius of AEsculapius who not having been able to save his life receives him & encourages him to enter AElysium - the figure of Pluto he supposes to be Minos, Oecus or Rhadamanthus as the gods never were represented in human attitudes and the muscles seem too strongly marked. But all this is I think much too fanciful & part of the merit of the vase is lost by restricting its signification to the particular story of a new married man.

The Princess desired to have a pair of bracelets which come to 14 guineas but they neither of them desired to subscribe to the vase - The Secretary Fagel who is an officer
of state & has a great Cabinet will I believe write a desire to be a subscriber to the vase.
Almost all the ladies had cameos mounted in one way or another.
The company left Lt Aucklands about 1/2 past 1 & we then put up our goods & came away.
I am going to dine with Lord Hy Spencer but Mr Byerley declined it as he must call on the Spanish ambassador who wants some ware.
Tomorrow morning we shall set out for Amsterdam & perhaps shall see Mr. Hopes great house in the way - we pass through Haarlaem & Leyden.

When you write next to Lt Auckland I hope you will express to him how much we are obliged to his Lordship for his very kind behaviour to us which nothing can exceed. His Lordship lives here in very great splendour & represents our nation with very great credit.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Sunday 18th off the island of Ameland. Dear Sir

We are now opposite the Island of Ameland north of the Texel which is remarkable by having something like hills upon it but they are only sand cast up. We have a vessel of about 70 feet in length to ourselves and expect to be at Embden tomorrow - it is now 1 o'clock.

July 19 - 7 o'clock. We have been very much disappointed in our expectations - with a very fine wind in our favour our lord the Skipper thought proper to come to anchor at a small island called Schiermonk almost opposite the mouth of the river Ems at 4 o'clock in the afternoon & contrary to his promise he staid there 16 hours. We went on shore in the afternoon & saw a well built little village with a church in it and all the inhabitants well dressed in the true dutch dress - we appeared to be fully as much objects of curiosity to them as they were to us and some of them were so diverted with our ridiculous appearance,
not having great breeches like sacks on, that they were obliged to turn aside to avoid laughing in our faces.

This little island is all sand but furnishes I believe corn butter and cheese enough for its inhabitants, at least so our boatman says. It has almost as many small sloops belonging to it as houses, & appears to be to Hamburg Amsterdam and the other towns on the coast what Holland is to the rest of the world - the men all live on the sea and our skipper had unfortunately for us a large family here who kept him here until 12 today instead of setting off at 2 or 3 in the morning as he promised. There are on this island horses cows hogs & fine rabbits in great abundance. We walked to the top of a ridge of sand hills which runs across the island and if they had not had some vegetables thinly scattered over them we might have imagined ourselves in one of Mr. Bruce's sandy deserts. We are now in the mouth of the Ems and have a sight of the German land but are afraid we shall not get to Embden tonight.
July 26.

We arrived here on Saturday night after travelling 24 hours without stopping longer than to change horses. We have called today on most of our friends but they are almost all of them at their gardens in the country for it is the fashion here as in Amsterdam & London for the merchants to go into the country on Saturday & not to return until Monday evening.

We have been settling the most proper way of showing the vase and have agreed to do as we did at Amsterdam at Veldhuysen's - that is to leave it at a very capital magazine of porcelain, earthen wares and furniture, where all the nobility and first people resort. We have done business with this house for 12 years without knowing their names before this summer. They have bought great quantities of enamelled goods through merchants hands in London. These gentlemen Philp. & Otto van Axen will write notes to all the principal people and enclose the descriptions. This arrangement obliges them and shows the vase to a much greater number of persons than we could possibly do in any other way. Mess. P. & O van Axen say that this is a place where the merchants are very rich and do not grudge
any expense in purchasing fine things, but they have no taste or judgment.

We have been endeavouring to find out the artificers who might be induced to use cameos and medallions, such as cabinet makers & inlayers & of these there are some very good ones & we shall I think do something in this way. We have seen an architect this morning who has been studying at Rome & he seems disposed to make use of our bas reliefs if there was a depot here that he could get what he may want. However I think that cannot be established; we shall very probably persuade Messrs van Axen to order a few & then those who want them must order them of the sizes & forms that they wish for.

When we were at Rotterdam we spoke with Bruley a jeweller & Grand l'aine` a merchant in french clocks & watches & they both seemed inclined to do something in cameos & jasper ornaments. Their fair is in the beginning of September & it is at that time that a new thing is best made known.
Would you not have us call on Lord Gower when we go to Paris. I believe all that is necessary is to leave ones name & that is expected from all the English.
