Mr. Byerley thinks that the price might very probably deter some people from subscribing as they seemed to think it a good deal of money - but the countries we have passed through do not abound with people who have any knowledge of, or love for, the arts.

Your next letters may be addressed to Berlin & I hope to have a letter there from some of my brothers & sisters with an account of the enlarged fish pool, the plantations &c. &c. We shall be at Berlin about the 8th of August.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Frankfurt, Octr 9 - 1790.

We make up a packet which we send to the Hague & beg Lord Auckland to forward by the Messenger - It contains an enamelled watch case & the guts which are taken out, & a model of a case with a small rim of brass ( lunette ).

These are given us by freres Melly one of the first houses at Geneva to whom we had a letter from Le Coq - they desired to know if we could make cases for them & wished to have an exclusive sale for some time. I have only to say that we engaged for the utmost secrecy & exactness & also that you should set about making the trials as soon as possible as they wish to bring them out next Leipsig fair -
The subjects which they like best are Merchant d'Amour - the 3 french subjects l'oracle d'amour & the two companions - Flaxmans sacrifice to Peace - And any others in the same stile - no boys -

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, April 12. 1791.
Dear Sir

As Mr Byerleys unfortunate state of health obliges him to live in the country & as it is necessary for him to go immediately it appears to be necessary that some person of confidence should immediately come into the house in Greek Street. As I do not at present know of anybody that would answer the description & that is disengaged I offer myself to stay in London until some proper person can be procured if you think I should be more useful there than here.

What I mean is that I would live in the house and take care of the correspondence while Mr B. is unfit for it, and do what other business I could, except attending in the rooms any farther than waiting upon some particular people, for I have been too long in the habit of looking upon myself as the equal of everybody to bear the haughty manners of those who come into a shop.
If I come I shall bring my horse up with me as an antidote to foul air & smoke.
This thought struck me on reading my mothers letter to Kitty and consequently I have not had much time to reflect upon it.

I am very glad to hear you mean to ride a good deal when you come home and I hope you will meet with a horse that will suit you better than your present one though he is by no means a bad one. When I proposed your selling I thought your dislike to him was the reason of your not having ridden much lately. As we have got the black mare into service again we can very well part with Silverlocks particularly as my sisters cannot ride him & he is too little for Tom.
I am Your dutiful & affect. son
J. Wedgwood junr.
Dear Sir

I cannot refrain from expressing to you the high satisfaction I have received from the kind & very honourable attention paid to you, on your late heavy misfortune, by the philosophers of Paris. I suppose their address will by this time have been presented to you, for the letter which mentions it to me, from Mr. Seguin is dated Augt. 10. though, from a mistake in the direction, it has been on the road
till now. He says, 'We have all taken a great part in the misfortune which has fallen upon M. Priestly; we esteem him in every point of view; & we are employed at this moment in drawing up a letter which is to be addressed to him by all the savants of the capital.' I persuade myself therefore that you will rise still more splendid & more respected from what was intended to sink you, & I am sure I not mistaken in what I have said to Mr. Seguin, that your calmness & magnanimity on this trying occasion have put your enemies to shame.

I should not hour have intruded upon you at present with a letter merely on this subject. Mess. Lavoisier & Seguin have requested some information from me, which I do not find myself very capable of supplying out of my own funds. They are constructing a furnace to be fed with vital air, in which they mean to melt 100 pounds of Platina, for the use of the commissaires appointed by the academy for the ascertaining of weights & measures. It was natural enough for them to apply to me on this occasion for clay of the most unfusible nature; but I know of none which possesses this property in a greater degree than the Stourbridge, and I am confident
that they have in France clays as refractory as this. Do you think, Sir, that these or any clays can stand the action of a fire with dephlogisticated air? You have had some experience on this subject; I have not.

Mr. Lavoisier has sent for two of my thermometers, which I have accordingly forwarded to him. Mr. Seguin says, 'We find this instrument of the greatest use, & at this moment feel more than ever its indispensibility; because we are occupying ourselves, Mr. Lavoisier & I, in completing the theory of furnaces of fusion.
I am with sincerest regard
Etruria Nov. 30. 1791
Dear Sir

I was duly favoured with your obliging letter of the 22d; & a copy of your Appeal , which you were so kind as to send for my perusal, came here on Sunday last (the 27th). I return you my sincere thanks for this & many other instances of your kind attention. A slight indisposition which is now pretty well over, & preparing for an intended journey,
have hitherto prevented my bestowing that time upon this work which it so well deserves; but I have read several times over a part of it which I sincerely wish was more universally distributed & read than it is likely to be whilst it continues only a small part of a large work. I therefore wish it was detached, & circulated as much as possible, provided there is no particular reason against it which I am unacquainted with. I mean the Address to you from your congregation, particularly the younger part of it, with your answers to them. If I may judge from my own feelings, these little pieces could not fail of having an admirable effect upon the minds of the rising generation; & even with persons of riper years might do more good, as they find a shorter way to the heart, than any merely argumentative pieces whatever.

As you desire my free thoughts, I will give you them as they arise in the course of my reading, only begging you will not expect me to enlarge upon, or even to mention, the parts which I admire, for in that case I should have a volume to write; I shall only point out a few instances where, if I had been present at the time of writing, I might have ventured to propose some alterations. I will begin with the Preface.

p. xxiv. I am very loath to admit the proposition. Indeed it seems hardly possible that the spirit either of the people or the government should be more intolerant than some of our laws are. Neither must we judge of the general spirit of the people from what has happened lately at Birmingham, in situations where half a score of noisy good-for-nothing fellows will obtrude themselves more upon the public notice than a thousand of the common orderly & worthy members of the community; & unless this circumstance is attended to & taken into account, we shall in all times of public disturbance & riot, make miserably wide estimates, & draw equally false conclusions from such principles.

But admitting the fact to be as stated, may not the holding it forth to public view tend rather to encourage & increase, than to diminish, such a spirit among the populace; for what can be more likely to inflame them still further, than a conviction of their having
numbers on their side, & of their acting with a majority?

xxxii. In works of mediocrity, & where the subject is not of itself highly interesting, such a species of spirit as this paragraph contains might not be amiss; but here both the author & his subject are above it, & I hope therefore that those parts of the paragraph which contain either general reflections or what may be deemed sarcasm, will be omitted or new modelled.

ibid.
May not this idea give a mischievous hint to some future mob? We only shaved his beard before, they will say; but now we will take his own advice, & do the business effectually.

54. I am not certain that I understand this passage. Government, it is true, has not been so kind to dissenters in some instances as to grant their requests, which we think it not only might have done with perfect safety, but ought to have done, we having a claim to it as a matter of right: we therefore say that government has not been friendly to us in these instances; but is it the same thing to say that government is not friendly to us , as that we are not friendly to government ? I think it will not be understood so, & that this will be considered as an acknowledgement of our not being now friendly, & consequently of our being inimical to the present government ; & when this is said by a person of Dr. Priestley's importance among the dissenters, it will be taken for granted that he has good grounds for the assertion, & that the majority at least
of dissenters are of this description. I must therefore say, that I either mistake, or disapprove, this expression.

69. I know nothing of the facts; but in my opinion, the bringing of the idea forward can do no good, & may be productive of much mischief. 'What! our enemies will be ready enough to say, are they begun to provide arms! then it is time for us to follow the example,' &c. &c. so that this single paragraph may serve for a declaration of war, & I hope it will be omitted.

84.
You cannot mean to admit that your enemies may with truth say this of you, for that must imply, that you wish our present constitution, not reformed , but overturned , as one cannot be set up , without the other being first set down , & I am, as I believe you are, very far from wishing to see either. I know there must be a mistake, either in the text or in my understanding of it, & I should be glad to know where the mistake lies.

I hope you will pardon the liberty I mean to take of keeping your Appeal a few days longer, that I may have time to read some parts over again. I have taken the liberty you gave me of offering my thoughts freely , as they are intended for your own inspection only.
Pray make my respectful complimts. to Mrs. Priestly, accept my best wishes for your health & happiness in your new situation, & believe me most sincerely
Dear Sir your very faithful & obedt. Served.
J. W.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, April 27, 1792.
Dear Sir

This morning we sent a requisition to the Surveyor not to proceed in making the road from Warners house but to go on from Stoke to T & in the afternoon the 6 who had given him the order to make from Warners repented & told him to go back again - so
consistent are they. I believe Fletcher was alarmed at the illegality of the proceedings & Hassells was so frightened the day after he had given the order that he begged Wolf would get 7 or 8 trustees immediately to contradict it.

Mr Fletcher is very desirous to bring about an accommodation by getting the road to Tunstall wall gate & I think the people of Stoke would be glad to agree to such a proposition. The arguments that weigh for it with me are the uncertainty of our having a majority at the next meeting, the extra expense which would attend the making of the road to Handford bridge & the probable risk of the road over the meadow at H. bridge not being quite secure from floods.
I send you a copy of the consents which Mr C. thinks Mr White should see.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO THOMAS WEDGWOOD.

text.p: Etruria, July 11. 1792.
Dear Tom
We begin to expect a letter from you announcing your arrival at Paris.

Our papers are full of apprehensions of mobs & great disturbances on the 14 July. They tell us that the Republican party become desperate & that they are doing all they can to incite the people to rise. Perhaps you do not know much more of the matter than we do but I daresay you find everything quiet at Paris. Our counties are still addressing the King on his Proclamation & I dare say there will not be one that will not give this proof of its loyalty.
Love & Compts to be distributed as proper.
I am sincerely Your affect brother
JW.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Tenby, Augt 20, 1792.
Dr Sir

You will have heard by a letter of mine to Tom that we have had a very gay week at Haverfordwest assizes. I have not been at Crossly since but as I left them all very well I hope to find them so tomorrow. The family at Crossly is altogether the most charming one I have ever been introduced to & their society makes no small addition to the pleasure I have received from this excursion. I am very happy to observe that their spirits are not much affected by their fathers marriage, I suppose however that it must raise some unpleasant reflections when they are alone.

Our pleasures here are very simple riding, walking & bathing, with a little dance twice a week. We have besides some excursions on the water which are very agreeable as the bay of Tenby is extremely beautiful & we have five of the band of the Pembroke militia who go out on such occasions.

You are so kind as to say that you shall be glad to see me & my sister but I hope you have no objection to our staying a while longer as much on my sisters account as my own, for I am afraid she has little chance of bringing Miss A. back with her.
Your affect & dutiful son
Josiah Wedgwood jr.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR.

text.p: Etruria, Feb. 6. 1793.
My Dear Jose.

We are going on with your house very well. I have planned a room over the kitchen, which will be 5 feet high on the walls, & leave the kitchen 12ft high, which is quite as high as ours, & as high as it should be. We are rather at a loss for bricks, but William is going a brick hunting by the canal to morrow morning. Give my love to your sister Susan, with my best wishes for her pleasant journey to Bath, & that she may find the water salutary - our love to all - the horn is blowing at the door.
I am Your affect. father
Jose. Wedgwood.
Pray bring the plan of the catacombs

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, April 15. 1793.
Dear Sir

Three black barberini vases are come out today, one of them very perfect as to staining, the other two are not so well fired, the stain instead of being of a bluish black is brown. They are all three very good in other respects, no blisters nor the figures or leaves risen in any part.

I should be much obliged if you would examine Johns forcing pump & tell me what you think of it. It is put up by Bramah. I applied to him to know the weight & expense of a pump of that sort sufficient to throw water about 50 feet high for the reservoir to my steam cooking apparatus. Bramah answered me that the price would be 8 guineas & the weight about 3 qrs. cwt. I must no doubt get the pipes cast here. I know that you have been obliged to take down your forcing pump though constructed by Whitehurst who was certainly a good mechanic. I have written to Bramah to know if he has adopted any new principle to prevent pipes bursting. If you
had time to call upon him perhaps you would ascertain the point. I have found a place for a garden much superior in every respect to the present one at my house. It is the corner of the field we have just taken from Billington. The soil is the best in this neighbourhood & 18 inches deep or 2 feet. The East & north winds are exceedingly well warded off by the plantation which borders two sides of this field & it lies open to the full influence of the mid-day sun. It is a very convenient distance from our house being only across the road & it is quite out of sight. I propose to build a cottage on the spot for the gardener who will defend it from depredation to which it would otherwise be subject.
I am your dutiful son
J W

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, April 22. 1793.
Dear Sir

This country now begins to feel the distress produced by the stagnation of trade.
Edd. Bourne has failed & as he has taken every means in his power of tempting persons to furnish him with cash by a high premium he has injured a great number of the little shopkeepers. Some others at Burslem are mentioned as likely to go such as Patin & the proprietor of the Bell work. I believe too that Ralph Wedgwood is tottering he has parted with many of his men. Joshua Heath & Ralph Mare are mentioned as not very stable & I dare say the other end of the Pottery is as ill supported.
Your affect. & dutiful son
Josiah Wedgwood.

note.value: JOSIAH WEDGWOOD JUNIOR TO JOSIAH WEDGWOOD SENIOR.

text.p: Etruria, Sepr. 10. 1793.
Dear Sir

Our old porter T. Woodal is very much tired of his life as a soldier & extremely desirous of obtaining his discharge - his health too is very bad. He would get two men in his place if that would do. I have told Sherratt who spoke to me about him that I did not suppose anything would procure his discharge but that the only way I knew of going about it was to apply to his officer & to enquire if he would discharge him on his procuring two others to serve for him.
I am Dear Sir Your grateful & dutiful son
Josiah Wedgwood Jr.
Liverpool, Octr. 11 1765.
Dr. Sir
Mr. Bentley never had the Pleasure of seeing Dr. Darwin, but shall think himself much honoured by his Friendship, & future Correspondence.

I am extremely concerned that your Remarks
did not come sooner; as Mr. Sparrow sent me the MS about a Month ago, desiring I would get it printed immediately; & telling me they could do nothing more till that was ready to put into peoples Hands

In every work that can bear the Expense I think it would always be prudent to print a few Copies with large Margins first, to put into the Hands of Critics. This is the only way of bringing a Work to any Degree of Correctness, as the Ears of Writers grow familiar with their own Expressions, be they ever so harsh or inelegant. I have found this by Experience, in a Considerable Work, which I transcribed for the Press, after the Corrections of a Hundred contending Critics; - no two of which were hardly ever of the same Opinion, about the Elegance of an Expression. Several of your Remarks on the first Section are very just, & some of the Passages have already been corrected nearly in the manner you propose. But if it be so full of Inelegancies as you think, it is to no Purpose to attend to Particulars. The Pamphlet can only, at best, appear as a Piece of Patch-work; - & ought to be all written over again. The Misfortune is, the first Sheet is printed off. I understood the
first Edition, as you call it, had nearly your Approbation; & therefore presumed that this which is a little more correct, & less pompous would have pleased you better; though I am far from thinking it is what it might have been if some Person better capable of Writing would have undertaken it. But the Misfortune is, those who can write best, seldom know much of such Subjects; & no man can ever write well upon a subject that he does not understand: - so that I think it no easy matter to find a proper Author for this Business; & if Dr. Darwin, Mr. Wedgwood, & your humble Servant, could have been altogether, I fancy they could have done it as well as anybody else.

I have not my Copy before me; but certainly that which you have is very imperfect, as several of the expressions you take notice of, are not in mine. The word Legislature means the Power that enacts Laws, & in english is a Noun of Multitude, including King, Lords, & Commons; & therefore I think is used properly. I know not what to do with the Pamphlet. The second Sheet is almost finished. I will make all the Use I can of your Remarks, & desire the Continuance of them . I am much pleased that Dr: Darwin permits me to call myself his obt. Friend & hble Served:
Those: Bentley.
Expanse of Water is so clear , in the Translation of Le Count, is neither the Sense of the Original, nor any Sense at all.
Liverpool, Octr., 15 1765.
Dr. Sir

It pleases me not a little, that I had corrected several of the Places you had taken notice of, almost exactly as you propose - & I approve, & have adopted almost all your Corrections that did not come too late.

The Article of China, I confess may appear, at the first reading, a little Hobby horsical: - but if you consider the Quotation was only introduced on acct of the Reservoir ; to show that the hint about watering the meadows was not chimerical; you will, I think, not be offended with the Mention of China again in another View : - And in a just Climax; as the Country's are considered in the Order in
which they have recd. Benefit from Inland Navigations: - & from all Accounts, no Country deserves to be attended to on this Subject so much as China, where navigable Canals do really produce most Wonderful Effects. I acknowledge the Propriety of your Distinction of Styles. I think the Language of such a Pamphlet as this should be plain & concise; with all the Elegance that the Subject admits of; but free from rhetorical Expressions; except in the Conclusion; - & even there I should be afraid of risking any thing very animated; for fear the Reader should suspect a Design to impose upon him; as the Readers of this Pamphlet will be looking out for Deceit and Artifice in every line of it, I would disappoint them, with the manly Simplicity of Truth.

I have wrote a Paragraph about the Coaling Trade, & the Security in Time of War, which I hope you will think properly guarded. I agree with you in disliking the Dedication. There must be one about that length. There are two Leaves left for the Title Page, & Dedication to be printed last. Pray send me a Sketch of one something different. I do not know how to mend this; & please to let me have it by the next Post. Poor Mr. Turner! His Lady cannot live many Days in
all probability; & I wish it does not kill him. He grieves extremely; - & has complained of an irregular Pulsation of his Heart which alarmed Us.
I hope for the Pleasure of seeing Dr. Darwin sometime, really , & am his very respectful & affectionate Frd, & hble Served.
Those: Bentley.
Mr. & Mrs. Turner are both a little better; but I doubt there is no reason to flatter ourselves with the Hopes of her Recovery.
Liverpool, Octr. 22: 1765.
Dr. Sir

When I recd. your first Letter I immediately wrote to Mr. Wedgwood, & told him you condemned the Pamplet, in its present
State, not to be printed . In Answer, I was desired to go on with it; as a Pamplet was immediately necessary; & he did not apprehend there was any thing materially wrong in this. When it was sent to me from Newcastle I was desired to have it printed with all possible Dispatch; & told that it was returned without Alteration, much approved. So that the Censure of me for haste is misapplied . I always desired the Thing might not be done hastily - & should never have engaged in it at all, but at the earnest Solicitation of my good Friend Mr. Wedgwood. Mr. Bentley is not afraid the Pamphlet should be improved: he heartily wishes it was much more perfect than it is; & doubts not but Dr: Darwin could have finished it in better manner, if he would have taken that Trouble upon himself which Mr: B understood he did not choose to do.

All my intimate Friends know how humbly I think of my own trifling Compositions; & how ready I am at all times to receive their Assistance & Corrections. But this Work is not mine. There are hardly two Paragraphs together of my writing in the whole; - & every one knows there is a great deal of difference between writing a Piece , & endeavouring to mend one.

You say the Liverpool Liturgy was not
read, because it was ill-written . And yet that Book was written by Gentlemen of as much Learning as any we shall find for this Pamphlet; & had all the Advantage of Reviewing (from which you seem to expect too much,) that a Work could have. It received the Corrections of Many Gentlemen who were as well qualified as any in this Kingdom for that Purpose; - & by many good Judges, it is thought to be excellently well written . So much do Men of Learning & Taste differ in their Judgments!

"It is no Discredit to Mr. Bentley, that he does not write agreeably & concisely. But it is no Credit to him that he does not know it." - How must a Man know this? It is the first Time he was ever told so: - & it is not a very easy Matter for any one to discover his own Faults. But, as Mr. Bentley does not presume to judge of Dr. Darwin's Manner of Writing from one Part of this Pamplet, so neither can Dr. Darwin judge of Mr. B's manner from the other . If a Pamphlet, that was written by Nobody; but is the joint work of several Persons, who had no opportunities of consulting together, proves, at last but a Piece of Patch-Work; - this Fault is rather to be attributed to the Circumstances , than to any of the Parties concerned in it. I have written
again to Mr. Wedgwood; & shall follow his Instructions. Perhaps it will be best to hand this Pamphlet about as an unfinished Copy ; - &, when it has recd. all the Advantages that Criticism can bestow upon it, to publish it.

I thank you for transcribing Mr. Garbet's Letter. I do not know an Object more worthy of the Attention of the Society in the Strand; & wish they may take Notice of it. I do not see any thing very material in the Remarks, but what has been attended to in the Pamphlet; though Birmingham might be made a larger Article, without much Impropriety. If the Lichfield Edition be different from the Ground-work of this Pamphlet, which was sent to me, I have never seen it.

If there is to be a rivalship between these two Editions, I resign with all humility & Pleasure. I am concerned for nothing but the general design , & am Dr. Darwin's very respectful Frd & hble Served
T. Bentley
